extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, journalists and researchers interested in Frankie Boyle and British comedy controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for what makes stand-up or televised/recorded comedy acceptable, broadcastable, and commercially successful, drawn from a biography of a high-profile UK comedian and the controversies around his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness / risk of offending the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Material may be judged 'humiliating' or as having 'risked offending the audience' by broadcasters or regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC rulings noted jokes that were 'humiliating' and 'risked offending the audience'; content can be deemed 'too offensive for broadcast' (e.g., compilations titled 'Too Hot for TV'). Use examples: Rebecca Adlington spoon joke, jokes about the Queen, Paralympics tweets. Offensiveness is a key input to editorial decisions and regulatory complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects that are off-limits or especially sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain targets (notably children, disabled people, victims) are treated as particularly sensitive and may be considered inappropriate subjects for jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaints and criticism centered on jokes about a disabled child (Harvey Price) and material referencing Down's syndrome; critics and organisations (e.g., Mencap) said comments could be misconstrued and tantamount to bullying. Broadcasters and public reaction indicate higher risk when jokes involve children or vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting rules compliance (Ofcom / BBC Trust standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy material must comply with broadcasting codes and editorial standards; regulators may rule whether material breaches rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ofcom investigated and ruled Channel 4 breached broadcasting rules in the Katie Price/Harvey material (but did not require an on-air apology). The BBC Trust assessed other jokes and described some comments as 'sexist and ageist' while clearing misconduct. Producers and broadcasters consider these standards when commissioning and airing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial judgment and producer/broadcaster control
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers and broadcasters exercise editorial control including cutting or editing material they judge problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: entire six-minute Comic Relief performance was cut from broadcast; Boyle accused BBC producers of 'editing out' comments. Editors balance creative freedom against audience, regulatory and reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and intent as a defence or rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians may defend controversial material by citing context, intent, or the larger argumentative routine rather than isolated lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle argued some jokes were intended to highlight exploitation (Katie Price) or formed part of a routine concluding certain jokes are a product of toxic masculinity (Holly Willoughby rape joke). Context may influence public and regulator interpretation, but is not always sufficient to avoid sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk and libel/defamation exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements and press coverage can lead to libel claims or threatened legal action, affecting a comedian's choices and repercussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle sued the Daily Mirror for libel and won damages; Katie Price and Peter Andre sought legal action and complained to Channel 4. Legal outcomes (libel damages, complaints) are a tangible risk metric for public commentary and published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience testing and iterative editing of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing material live and editing based on audience reaction is a practice for assessing what to include in broadcasts or recorded specials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle's 'Mock the Week Musings' podcast recorded him testing material and noting certain jokes 'are not going into the show due to their reaction (or lack thereof)'. Comedians often trial jokes and adjust content before formal broadcast or release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of explicit-content warnings and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling material as explicit or carrying content warnings is a practice to signal potentially offensive material to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The podcast carried an explicit content warning. Warnings help set audience expectations and may mitigate some editorial concerns, but do not remove regulatory responsibility or public criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success and audience demand as performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ticket sales, sold-out runs, DVD/streaming releases and tour extensions indicate market success and can be used to evaluate a comedian's impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sold-out runs, extended tours, DVD releases, Netflix exclusives and large-scale tours were listed as measures of Boyle's commercial success. These are outcome metrics distinct from acceptability or regulatory compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public controversy and reputational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversial jokes can generate complaints, media backlash, removal from broadcasts, or damage/control of reputation for the comedian and broadcasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents led to Ofcom investigations, broadcast edits, removal from events (e.g., Comic Relief cut), and sustained media coverage. Reputation effects include criticism from MPs, charities, and public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing free expression with public sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an evaluative tension between protecting free expression/pushing boundaries and respecting public standards and sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle criticised the BBC as 'cravenly afraid of giving offence' and defended boundary-pushing as part of comedy, while regulators and parts of the public demanded restraint. Decisions often reflect institutional risk tolerance and prevailing social norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection: punching up vs punching down considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Who the joke targets (powerful institutions/figures vs vulnerable individuals/groups) influences judgments about appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much controversy arose when jokes appeared to target vulnerable individuals (disabled child) as opposed to powerful public figures; critics framed some material as 'bullying' while defenders framed other material as criticism of institutions or public figures (e.g., politicians, monarchy, state actions). Evaluators consider whether comedy 'punches up' or 'punches down'.
